opts: Waiting for spontaneous separation and expulsion, with more blood loss and a higher risk of PPH
A uterotonic within one minute of the birth, followed by controlled cord traction
Controlled cord traction with suprapubic counter-pressure and early clamping of the cord
Early cord clamping with immediate traction on the cord to hasten separation of the placenta
exp: Passive management means waiting for signs of separation without a uterotonic; it increases blood loss, PPH and maternal mortality.

opts: Pulmonary stenosis or atresia, ventricular hypertrophy and predominantly right-sided dysfunction
Left ventricular hypoplasia with a small aortic root and coarctation
An isolated ventricular septal defect with no myocardial hypertrophy at all
A structurally and functionally normal heart in the great majority of recipient twins
exp: The recipient twin is volume loaded, so the right side bears the brunt: pulmonary stenosis or atresia, hypertrophy and right-sided dysfunction.

opts: Intrapartum benzyl penicillin, with ampicillin or cefazolin and clindamycin if she is penicillin-allergic
Antepartum oral erythromycin given for a week before the expected date of delivery
Postpartum metronidazole started once the placenta has been delivered
Intrapartum gentamicin alone as a single intramuscular injection
exp: Prophylaxis must be intrapartum to clear carriage at delivery: benzyl penicillin, with alternatives for allergy.

opts: Resuscitation alone, since surgery is never indicated once the tube has ruptured
Expectant and medical management, and any operation short of salpingectomy
Laparotomy, which is contraindicated in favour of a laparoscopic approach
Salpingectomy, which must always be avoided in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy
exp: Once rupture has occurred with instability, expectant and medical treatment are contraindicated and the bleeding tube must be removed.

opts: Excessive or prolonged bleeding with a uterus larger than expected for the postpartum day
Amenorrhoea with a small, well-involuted uterus on bimanual examination
High fever with a closed cervical os and no lochia being passed at all
A painless white discharge with itching and no abnormal bleeding
exp: Subinvolution presents as prolonged or excessive lochia with a uterus that is bigger and softer than it should be for the day.

opts: About 1.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about three percentage points
About 0.2 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about one percentage point
About 3.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about nine percentage points
About 5.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about fifteen percentage points
exp: A rough rule is that one unit of packed cells raises the haemoglobin by about 1 g/dL and the haematocrit by about 3 per cent.

opts: The type of previous incision, the number of previous caesareans and the inter-delivery interval
Maternal age alone, which determines the tensile strength of the uterine scar
Fetal sex and birth weight, since a large baby stretches the scar in labour
The placental site alone, because a fundal placenta weakens the lower segment
exp: Rupture risk tracks the scar itself — a classical scar, multiple scars and a short inter-delivery interval all raise it.

opts: Safer and easier to apply; pressure starts at 0.2 kg/cm2 and is raised to 0.8 kg/cm2 over about two minutes
Metal cups that are more traumatic, built up to 1.5 kg/cm2 over ten minutes
Rigid cups applied to a pressure of 0.5 kg/cm2 reached instantly
Disposable cups with the maximum pressure limited to 0.1 kg/cm2
exp: Silastic cups cause less scalp trauma and are applied with negative pressure rising gradually to 0.8 kg/cm2 (600 mmHg).

opts: Flexion in breech and face presentation; caesarean for transverse lie, mento-posterior face and brow
Flexion in vertex presentation; caesarean for a persistent occipito-posterior position
Flexion in brow presentation; caesarean for a left mento-anterior face presentation
Flexion in every presentation, with caesarean section never actually mandatory
exp: Breech and face deliver by flexion; transverse lie, persistent mento-posterior and brow presentation cannot deliver vaginally.

opts: Bleeding, need for transfusion, uterine rupture, hysterectomy and fetal distress or death
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn from delayed clearance of lung fluid
Anaesthetic risk alone, since labour itself adds no measurable risk
Placenta previa in the index pregnancy or in any later pregnancy
exp: A trial of labour trades anaesthetic and respiratory risk for rupture, haemorrhage and intrapartum fetal compromise.

opts: Monochorionic survivors are at risk through the shared anastomoses; dichorionic survivors largely are not
Both monochorionic and dichorionic survivors are at equal risk of neurological injury
Dichorionic survivors are at greater risk, because the second placenta also fails
Neither twin is at any risk once one of them has died in utero
exp: Acute transfusion through anastomoses at the moment of death is what injures the monochorionic survivor's brain.

opts: Ebstein anomaly, with downward displacement of the tricuspid leaflets
Tetralogy of Fallot, with an overriding aorta and pulmonary stenosis
Coarctation of the aorta, with hypertension confined to the upper limbs
Patent ductus arteriosus, with a continuous machinery murmur
exp: Lithium in cardiac organogenesis is classically linked to Ebstein anomaly, where the tricuspid leaflets are displaced into the right ventricle.

opts: The ammoniacal smell of urine, and dribbling seen on coughing after the bladder is emptied
The colour of the fluid, which is reliably yellow for urine and clear for liquor
The volume passed, since urine is always lost in a single large gush
The characteristic sweet odour of amniotic fluid on the bed linen
exp: Emptying the bladder with a catheter and then watching for further loss on coughing separates urine from amniotic fluid.

opts: Fever, subinvolution and uterine tenderness with offensive lochia; broad-spectrum antibiotics
Painless bleeding with a well-involuted uterus; evacuation of retained products
Profound shock with a flaccid uterus; emergency hysterectomy
Secondary amenorrhoea with hot flushes; hormonal replacement therapy
exp: Endometritis presents with postpartum pyrexia, a tender poorly involuted uterus and offensive lochia, and is treated with antibiotics.

opts: Leave the placenta in situ with the cord ligated at its insertion and close the hysterotomy
Immediate hysterectomy, whatever the woman's wishes about future fertility
Manual piecemeal removal of the placenta until the cavity is empty
Vigorous curettage of the placental bed to remove all adherent tissue
exp: Conservative management leaves the placenta in place; forced removal is what turns a controlled situation into a haemorrhage.

opts: At least ten discrete movements within two hours while resting in the left lateral position
At least three discrete movements recorded in any twenty-four hour period
At least twenty discrete movements recorded within a single hour
At least one discrete movement every ten minutes, by day and by night
exp: The Cardiff count-to-ten asks the woman to note the time to ten movements; fewer than ten in 12 hours, or a clear slowing, warrants testing.

opts: Massage with tranexamic acid and oxytocin, then methylergometrine, then carboprost, with misoprostol as an add-on
Carboprost first, then oxytocin, then methylergometrine in that order
Misoprostol first, then oxytocin, then carboprost in that order
Methylergometrine first, then misoprostol, then oxytocin in that order
exp: Oxytocin with tranexamic acid and massage is first line; ergometrine and then carboprost follow, with misoprostol as an adjunct.

opts: Anencephaly, anything preventing flexion such as a tight cord, and a roomy multiparous uterus
Hydrocephalus, a primigravid uterus and an android pelvis
Oligohydramnios with fetal growth restriction in a primigravida
Placenta previa with a gynaecoid pelvis and a well-flexed head
exp: Face presentation needs extension: anencephaly, a nuchal cord or neck mass that blocks flexion, and a lax multiparous uterus.

opts: Diabetes, Rh-negative pregnancy, twins, a succenturiate lobe and placenta bilobata
Pregnancy-induced hypertension and maternal thrombophilia
Folic acid deficiency with severe maternal anaemia
Cocaine abuse with the placental infarction it produces
exp: A bulky placenta covers more of the lower segment, so conditions that enlarge the placenta predispose to previa.

opts: The buttocks engage in the right oblique diameter and the anterior buttock rotates forward under Hart's rule
The buttocks engage in the antero-posterior diameter and rotate through two-eighths of a circle
The sacrum engages transversely and rotates through three-eighths of a circle
The buttocks engage in the left oblique diameter and descend without any rotation
exp: With the sacrum anterior the buttocks engage in the right oblique diameter and the anterior buttock descends and rotates forwards.

opts: Attending a single lecture on the MTP Act and its recent amendments
Completing a twenty-four hour online course on termination techniques
No specific clinical training is required of a registered medical practitioner
Assisting at 25 terminations and performing 5, or six months of house job in obstetrics and gynaecology
exp: The Act requires practical training: assisting at 25 procedures and performing 5, or an equivalent period of obstetric training.

opts: Twin pregnancy, gestational diabetes, polyhydramnios, macrosomia and a fibroid uterus
A bicornuate uterus, which overdistends and weakens the myometrium
Cervical incompetence with a short painless cervix in the second trimester
A uterine septum, which stretches the lower segment during pregnancy
exp: Overdistension of the uterus exhausts the myometrium; congenital anomalies do not overdistend it, though they can predispose otherwise.

opts: Repeat replacement under anaesthesia with a uterine relaxant, then Huntington's or Haultain's abdominal route
Immediate hysterectomy, since further attempts at replacement are futile
Hydrostatic reduction by O'Sullivan's method followed by Spinelli's vaginal repair
Vaginal packing with an oxytocin infusion to contract the uterus down
exp: If Johnson's vaginal replacement fails, the next attempt needs anaesthesia and a relaxant, with abdominal routes as the fallback.

opts: Frank breech lowest, complete breech low, knee presentation higher and footling highest
Frank breech highest, complete breech next, knee lower and footling presentation lowest
The risk of cord prolapse is identical for all four types of breech presentation
Complete breech highest, footling next, knee lower and frank breech lowest
exp: Cord prolapse risk rises as the presenting part fits the cervix less well: frank breech is snug, footling breech is not.

opts: Intracranial haemorrhage is the commonest cause of death, with asphyxia and intra-abdominal injury
Shoulder dystocia is the commonest cause of death, with brachial plexus injury
Erb's palsy is the commonest cause of death, from traction on the extended arms
Fracture of the femur is the commonest cause of death in vaginal breech delivery
exp: Rapid decompression and trapping of the after-coming head cause intracranial haemorrhage, the leading cause of death in breech.

opts: Caesarean section, instrumental delivery, prolonged labour and shoulder dystocia
Postpartum haemorrhage alone, with no effect on the mode of delivery
Malpresentation alone, with no increase in operative delivery
Prelabour rupture of membranes alone, with no intrapartum complications
exp: Macrosomia raises the whole spectrum of obstructed labour complications, including shoulder dystocia and operative delivery.

opts: A previous vaginal delivery is the best favourable marker; previous puerperal sepsis is a bad one
Young maternal age is the best favourable marker; a macrosomic fetus is a bad one
A male fetus is the best favourable marker; a twin pregnancy is a bad one
Short maternal stature is the best favourable marker; post-term pregnancy is a bad one
exp: Previous vaginal delivery, especially after a caesarean, predicts success; infection in the uterine scar predicts failure and rupture.

opts: Up to 200 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 600 mg per week
Up to 1000 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, with no weekly ceiling
Up to 50 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 200 mg per week
Up to 200 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 2000 mg per week
exp: Iron sucrose is given in divided doses: a maximum of 200 mg per day infused over 15-30 minutes and 600 mg per week.

opts: Thiamine 100 mg intravenously, to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy
Folic acid 5 mg intravenously, to prevent a megaloblastic crisis
Vitamin K 10 mg intravenously, to correct the coagulopathy
Vitamin C 500 mg intravenously, to hasten tissue healing
exp: Prolonged vomiting with confusion means thiamine must be given before any glucose, or Wernicke's encephalopathy follows.

opts: History and abdominal examination followed by a transabdominal screening ultrasound
Direct transvaginal scanning before any clinical assessment is made
Emergency caesarean section on the basis of the presenting complaint alone
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to map the placental site
exp: Transabdominal screening comes first; transvaginal scanning is then used to measure the placental edge when needed.

opts: Named for the mother's left and right; held correctly the left socket faces up and the right socket faces down
Named for the operator's hands, with both sockets facing upwards when applied
Identified by blade length, since the left blade is noticeably longer
Identified by colour coding on the handle of each blade
exp: Forceps blades are named for the side of the mother's pelvis; held correctly, the left blade's socket faces upwards.

opts: Hypotension, tachycardia and arrhythmias; and water intoxication from its antidiuretic effect
Severe hypertension with intracranial haemorrhage; and hyperglycaemia
Reflex bradycardia with heart block; and hypernatraemia from the salt load
High fever with rigors; and hypokalaemia from intracellular shift
exp: An intravenous bolus of oxytocin causes hypotension and arrhythmias, and large volumes of 5% dextrose cause water intoxication.

opts: Non-breastfeeding: combined pills avoided for 21 days — breastfeeding: progestogen-only before an intrauterine device
Combined pills are preferred in both groups from the first postpartum day
An intrauterine device only for non-breastfeeding women, and nothing at all for breastfeeding women
Injectable progestogen only for non-breastfeeding women, and combined pills for breastfeeding women
exp: Combined pills are avoided for 21 days because of thrombosis risk and they reduce milk supply; progestogen-only methods suit breastfeeding.

opts: Oxytocin acts on both segments and is used for induction and AMTSL; ergometrine is only used after delivery
Oxytocin acts on the lower segment alone and is used for PPH; ergometrine induces labour
Oxytocin acts on the upper segment alone and is used for induction; ergometrine is first line for induction
Oxytocin ripens the cervix; ergometrine acts on the fundus and is used for augmentation
exp: Oxytocin acts on the whole uterus and is used before and after delivery; ergometrine is used only after the baby is born.

opts: Not seen in humans; theoretically possible only until the cavity is obliterated at 14-16 weeks
Common after in vitro fertilisation, when several embryos are transferred
Seen only in multiparous women, who have a larger uterine cavity
The same as superfecundation, where two ova of one cycle are fertilised
exp: Superfetation would need a second ovulation and fertilisation after a pregnancy is established, which the decidua prevents.

opts: Retained placental fragments are commonest, then infection and incompletely remodelled vessels
Infection is commonest, with uterine fibroids the next most frequent cause
Anaemia is commonest, and breastfeeding delays involution further
Multiparity is commonest, with maternal obesity the next cause
exp: Retained products are the commonest cause; breastfeeding releases oxytocin and actually helps the uterus to involute.
